title: Read the Gauge
idea: Work out what one step on a scale is worth before reading it, keep the full calculator value, and round once at the end to three significant figures, counting from the first non-zero digit.
misconceptions: Counts squares as units when each square is worth more or less than one
Mixes up significant figures and decimal places
Rounds in two steps: 2.0449 becomes 2.045, then 2.05
Gives too few significant figures, such as dropping a needed final zero

estimate.basis: 150 spoken words a minute, plus each pause, 0.8 s for each cue and 2 s for each tap question with its longer feedback line. The two figures are the two recall versions; with no prerequisite explainer there is one recall version, so they are the same. Player turns are player-paced and not counted.

notes: Foundations is prior learning (FAL-953), so this runs 4–6 minutes, not 6–8, and some sections are short.

No prerequisite explainer. The recall section is one tap question on what students bring from earlier school (rounding to one decimal place), with no callback line, so it has a single `beats` list instead of `watched` and `not_watched`, and both length figures are the same.

No second-method section: the map lists no methods. Of the question type's methods, grid-count, first-nonzero-digit and round-once are the lesson; decimal places appears only as the contrast in example 2; plotting across-then-up and bounds are left to the question type.

The board is text only, so a gauge is written as its two labelled marks and the number of steps between them. A drawn gauge or axis would teach the scale better. That needs a figure board item, which the format doesn't have yet; raised on FAL-953 for phase 2.
The misconception "Plots (x, y) as (y, x)" belongs to plotting, which this script doesn't teach.

Example 3 is a two-part course-style item (a reading, then a GDC value given to 3 s.f.), as FAL-953 allows for Foundations. Its volume formula is given in the question, so no area-and-volume knowledge is needed.
Live numbers for the turns come from fn-pre-graph-reading (game/engine/situations/graph_reading.gd); the fallbacks are fixed and worked below.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Tess here. Every machine in this yard has a gauge on it, eh, and no two gauges agree on anything.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: The boiler counts in fours, the fuel tank counts in two point fives, and the water tank counts in whatever mood it's in that day.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: So today: read any gauge, and write the number down with the right number of figures.

board.write: Read it right. Round it once.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: First, one you brought with you from school. Tap the answer.

right.speaker: tin-can-tess
right.say: Three point five. The seven after the four rounds it up.

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: Look at the next digit along. It's a seven, which is five or more, so the four goes up to five. Three point five.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: First, the scale. Here's the boiler gauge. Two marks with numbers on, twenty and forty, and five small steps between them.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Never assume a step is worth one. Work it out: forty take twenty is twenty, and that's shared over five steps, so each step is four.

board.write: scale: what one step is worth

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: The needle sits three steps past twenty. Three fours, twelve, so the reading's thirty-two.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Now, rounding. A GDC gives you heaps of digits, more than anybody measured, and most answers want three significant figures.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Significant figures start at the first digit that isn't zero. Count three from there, then look at the next one. Five or more, and the last figure goes up.

board.write: significant figures: count from the first non-zero digit

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: One point four nine seven two, to three significant figures. One, four, nine, and the next digit is a seven, so the nine goes up. That makes one point five zero.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Keep the zero on the end. One point five is only two significant figures. The zero says you measured that far.

board.write: 1.5 is only 2 s.f., so keep the 0

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: And you round once, at the very end, from the full value the GDC gave you.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: My nan rounded everything. Her prices, her age, her recipes. Her scones were famous, for all the wrong reasons.

problem.setup: A fuel gauge has marks labelled 10 litres and 20 litres, with 4 equal steps between them. The needle is 3 steps past the 10 litre mark. Find the reading.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Here's the fuel tank. Step one: what we're finding, which is the amount of fuel in it, in litres.

board.write: Find the fuel reading, in litres.
board.label: Step 1: what are we finding?

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Step two: the givens. Marks at ten litres and twenty litres, four steps apart. The needle's three steps past ten.

board.write: Marks: 10 L and 20 L, 4 steps apart
board.label: Step 2: the givens

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Step three: what's one step worth? Twenty take ten is ten, over four steps. Each step is two point five litres.

board.label: Step 3: what is one step worth?

ask.prompt: Why not count each step as 1 litre?
choices: It would make the answer bigger

right.speaker: tin-can-tess
right.say: Right. The marks tell you what the steps are worth. Don't assume.

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: Look at the marks. Ten litres from one to the next, over four steps. So each step is more than one.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Step four: read it. Ten, plus three steps of two point five. Seventeen point five litres.

board.label: Step 4: count on from the mark

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Check: the needle's past halfway between ten and twenty, and so is seventeen point five.

board.write: Check: 3 of 4 steps is past halfway, and 17.5 > 15 ✓

intro.speaker: tin-can-tess
intro.say: Your go. Work out what one step is worth before you read anything.

fallback.setup: A pressure gauge has marks labelled 20 and 40, with 4 equal steps between them. The needle is 3 steps past the 20 mark.
working: Check: 3 of 4 steps is past halfway, and 35 > 30 ✓

right.speaker: tin-can-tess
right.say: Scale first, then the count. That's the way.

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: What's one step worth? Share the gap between the marks over the steps.

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: Count on from the labelled mark, not from zero.

problem.setup: A GDC gives the thickness of a sheet of tin as 0.0045678 metres. Write the thickness correct to 3 significant figures.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Now a small one. My GDC says this sheet of tin is zero point zero zero four five six seven eight metres thick, which is thin enough to see through, nearly.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: The zeros at the front only put the decimal point in the right place. They don't count. Start at the four.

board.write: 0.0045678: the first non-zero digit is the 4

right.speaker: tin-can-tess
right.say: Zero point zero zero four five seven. Four, five, six, and the seven after them rounds the six up.

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: Start counting at the four: four, five, six. The next digit is a seven, so the six goes up. Zero point zero zero four five seven.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Three decimal places would give zero point zero zero five. That's only one significant figure, and it throws away most of what the GDC told you.

problem.setup: A water tank is a cylinder of radius 0.9 m. Its depth gauge has marks labelled 1.0 m and 1.5 m, with 5 equal steps between them, and the needle is 3 steps past the 1.0 m mark. The volume of water in the tank is V = π × 0.9² × d m³, where d is the depth in metres.

parts.text: Write down the depth of the water.
Find the volume of water in the tank. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: This one's laid out like the exam papers. Two parts, so write the letters down as you go.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: The tank's a cylinder, radius zero point nine metres. The gauge has marks at one metre and one point five, five equal steps between them, and the needle's three steps past the one. The volume, V, is pi, times zero point nine squared, times the depth d.

board.write: gauge: 1.0 m to 1.5 m in 5 equal steps
V = π × 0.9² × d m³, d = depth in m

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Part a says write down. The marks are half a metre apart, over five steps, so a step is zero point one. Three steps past one metre is one point three metres.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Part b says find. Formula first, then the depth goes in.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: On the GDC that's three point three zero eight zero nine, and it keeps going. Write down what it gives you, with dots on the end.

ask.prompt: Why write 3.30809… and round only at the end?
choices: Rounding early can change the last figure

right.speaker: tin-can-tess
right.say: Yes. Round once, at the end, from the full value.

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: Every early rounding nudges the number a little. Do it a few times and the last figure moves. So you round once, at the end.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Three significant figures: three, three, zero, and the next digit is an eight. So the zero goes up. Three point three one cubic metres.

board.write: The tank holds 3.31 m³ of water.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: This is from my own log book, from before I knew better. One line's off. Which?

ask.prompt: Tap the line with the slip.

right.speaker: tin-can-tess
right.say: That's it. I rounded a number that was already rounded.

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: Look at the last line. Which number did I round from: the GDC's, or my own?

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Here's the check. Go back to the full value, two point zero four four nine. Three figures: two, zero, four. The next digit is a four, so nothing goes up. Two point zero four.

board.write: Check: 2.0449, and the digit after 2.04 is a 4, so 2.04 ✓

intro.speaker: tin-can-tess
intro.say: Your go, and no help on the first try. Scale first, and round once, at the end.

fallback.setup: A tank is a cylinder of radius 0.6 m. Its depth gauge has marks labelled 0 m and 2 m, with 8 equal steps between them, and the needle is 5 steps past 0. The volume of water is V = π × 0.6² × d m³, where d is the depth in metres.

parts.text: Write down the depth of the water.
Find the volume of water in the tank. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

right.speaker: tin-can-tess
right.say: Parts labelled, and rounded once at the end. That'd hold.

right.speaker: tin-can-tess
right.say: Heaps better than I did my first time.

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: What's one step worth? Work that out before you read the needle.

not_yet.speaker: tin-can-tess
not_yet.say: Round from the full GDC value, not from one you've already rounded.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: So. Before you read a gauge, work out what one step is worth. Keep every digit the GDC gives you, and round once, at the end, counting from the first digit that isn't zero.

board.write: one step = (gap between the marks) ÷ (number of steps)
3 s.f.: start at the first non-zero digit
Round once, at the end, from the full value

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: Mags wants every answer in her book to three significant figures, so you'll be using this next door.

beats.speaker: tin-can-tess
beats.say: That water tank gauge, by the way? Fixed it. The mood turned out to be a moth.
